Chapter 8: The Struggle for Recognition and the Politics of Visibility
Recognition really is one of our most basic needs. It’s that deep desire to be seen, to be acknowledged, to have your reality affirmed by others. But for so many people, recognition isn’t easy. It’s often hard-won, always a little incomplete, and sometimes it feels like it could vanish at any moment.
Think about this: the struggle to be visible isn’t just about catching someone’s attention. It’s about being understood, and being understood on your own terms.
Picture this memory for a moment. There’s a student in class, hand raised, eager to say something. But the teacher calls on someone else. That student’s hand drops, and the moment slips by... but the feeling? That sticks around. It’s not simply about being overlooked—it’s about feeling invisible.
Out in the world, the politics of visibility play out on a much bigger stage. Imagine the streets filled with protestors, their voices rising together, demanding to be heard. The media shows up, cameras rolling, but the story that gets told? Sometimes it’s not the story those protestors wanted to share. Their message is filtered, maybe even distorted.
Here’s the risk—visibility can end up being just another way people are erased. It becomes a spectacle, something that actually hides the real issues underneath.
On a personal level, the need for recognition is rarely simple. There’s a kind of pride in being seen, but also a real fear. When you’re visible, you’re open to scrutiny, and that can bring backlash. Some people decide it’s safer to keep their heads down, to avoid the spotlight. But others? They step right into it, determined to claim their space, no matter what it costs.
Even in families and close communities, this struggle shows up in all kinds of ways. A parent tries to share their experience with their child, searching for the right words that might make sense. A friend listens, nods along, but just doesn’t quite get it. That gap—the space between being seen and being truly known—can feel huge.
And yet, there are those rare, powerful moments when recognition is real. Maybe a teacher finally hears a student’s voice. Or a protester’s words reach someone who really needed to hear them. Or a friend simply says, “I see you,” and you know they mean it. These moments are rare, but they matter so much.
They give us a glimpse of what’s possible when we look past assumptions and really, honestly see each other.
The politics of visibility are complicated—shaped by power, by history, by who gets to decide what’s seen and what’s ignored. But this need for recognition? It never goes away. At the heart of every struggle, there’s that deep desire: to be seen—not as a symbol, but as a person.
